title: Routing and Data Fetching
summary: Client-side routing intercepts the browser's own navigation to keep an SPA feeling instant, and the fetch-on-render vs render-as-you-fetch spectrum determines whether that navigation waterfalls its data requests or parallelizes them.

slides.markdown:
A traditional multi-page site gets routing for free: click a link, the browser requests a new HTML document, the whole page reloads. A single-page app has to **fake that behavior** — intercept the click, update the URL, swap the visible component tree — without ever letting the browser do its default full navigation, or you lose all the client-side state an SPA exists to preserve.

Once routing works, the next question is almost always "when does data load relative to navigation?" — and that's where most real-world sluggishness in SPAs actually comes from: not the routing mechanism itself, but a chain of components each fetching only after its parent has already rendered, one request waiting on the next.

This topic covers both halves: how client-side routing actually intercepts navigation, and the fetch-on-render vs render-as-you-fetch spectrum that determines whether your app's data requests run in parallel or in a slow, invisible waterfall.

Client-side routers work by **preventing the browser's default navigation** and manually managing URL and page state instead, using two browser APIs:

- **`history.pushState(state, "", url)`** changes the URL shown in the address bar and adds a new entry to the browser's history stack, **without** triggering a page reload or a network request.
- **The `popstate` event** fires when the user clicks the browser's back/forward buttons, telling the router "the user navigated — figure out what to render for this URL now."

On a link click, the router calls `event.preventDefault()` to stop the browser's normal full-page navigation, then calls `pushState` to update the URL, then re-renders the component tree to match the new route — all without the browser ever requesting a new HTML document. This is the entire mechanical basis of every client-side router; libraries like React Router and Vue Router are convenience layers over exactly these two primitives.

slides.subTitle: Matching URL segments to component trees
slides.markdown:
Modern routers match a URL to a **tree** of components, not a single one — each segment of the path can correspond to a layer of the layout, and layers that don't change across a navigation don't need to re-render or remount.

For `/dashboard/settings/billing`, a typical router matches: `/dashboard` → a `DashboardLayout` (persistent sidebar, header), `/settings` → a `SettingsLayout` (nested tabs) nested inside it, and `/billing` → the actual `BillingPage` content nested inside that. Navigating from `/dashboard/settings/billing` to `/dashboard/settings/profile` only swaps the innermost segment — the `DashboardLayout` and `SettingsLayout` shells, and any state they hold (like a preserved scroll position or an open sidebar), are untouched.

This nested matching is why route-based code-splitting works cleanly: each segment can lazy-load only its own component, and a shared layout that's already loaded and rendered doesn't get re-fetched or re-rendered just because a child segment changed.

Three strategies for when data-fetching starts relative to rendering, in increasing order of how early the fetch kicks off:

| Strategy | When the fetch starts | Downside |
|---|---|---|
| **Fetch-on-render** | inside a component's effect, after it mounts | the component has to render once with no data, then again once data arrives — and a child can't start its own fetch until its parent has rendered and fired its own effect first |
| **Fetch-then-render** | before rendering starts at all, at the top of a route change | no premature empty render, but the user sees nothing (a blank screen or a route-level spinner) until every needed request finishes |
| **Render-as-you-fetch** | the fetch and the render are kicked off **at the same time**, as soon as the route is known | the UI can render its static shell immediately and stream in each piece of data as its own request resolves, independently |

The practical difference shows up as either a chain of round trips (fetch-on-render, if not restructured) or one blocking wait (fetch-then-render) versus overlapping, independent requests (render-as-you-fetch) — the next slide shows exactly what that looks like as a request timeline.

slides.subTitle: Coordinating multiple async boundaries
slides.markdown:
Once data-fetching is parallelized, a new coordination problem appears: several independent pieces of a page finish loading at different times, and naively rendering each as it resolves can produce a page that pops in piece by piece in a jarring, unpredictable order.

Suspense-style APIs (React's `<Suspense>`, and equivalents like Vue's `<Suspense>` component) solve this by letting a component **declare that it isn't ready yet**, and having the nearest ancestor `Suspense` boundary show a fallback (a spinner, a skeleton) until everything inside it resolves — all at once, rather than in a scattered sequence. Multiple independent fetches inside one boundary can run fully in parallel while still presenting as a single coordinated loading state to the user.

The design lever this gives you: where you place boundaries controls the *granularity* of loading states — one boundary around the whole page means a single spinner and one "pop in" moment; several nested boundaries mean the shell appears immediately while individual sections stream in independently, each with its own fallback.

slides.sectionTitle: A route loader fetching before rendering the page
A child fetching only after its parent finishes
Routing and data loading across frameworks
slides.markdown:
| | React | Vue | Next.js / Nuxt (meta-frameworks) |
|---|---|---|
| **Router** | React Router, TanStack Router | Vue Router | file-based routing built in |
| **Data loading primitive** | route `loader` functions, or framework-level server components | route-level `beforeEnter`/`asyncData` guards, or Pinia stores fetched on navigation | server-rendered `getServerSideProps`/`loader`, or `useAsyncData` — fetch happens before the client even receives HTML |

Meta-frameworks push render-as-you-fetch even further: because the data fetch can happen **on the server**, before any HTML reaches the browser at all, the client never sees a loading state for that data on first load — it's already embedded in the initial HTML response. This is the same underlying principle (start the fetch as early as possible, don't gate it behind a component mounting) taken to its logical extreme.

A strong answer to "this page takes too long to show data after navigating" moves through the same checklist every time:

1. **Open the network waterfall** (browser devtools) during the navigation and look for requests that start only after a previous one finished, rather than overlapping.
2. **Check whether a child component's mount is gated behind a parent's fetch resolving**, when the child's own request doesn't actually need data from that parent — the structural waterfall from this topic's pitfall slide.
3. **Check whether the fetch is tied to component mount at all**, versus starting as soon as the route itself is known — a route loader (or server-side fetch, in a meta-framework) removes an entire render-then-fetch round trip that a `useEffect`-based fetch can't avoid.
4. **Decide on loading-state granularity deliberately** — one Suspense boundary around the whole page trades a single, longer blank state for simplicity; several nested boundaries let the shell and fast data show immediately while slower pieces stream in independently.

Naming the waterfall by its actual mechanism — an unnecessary mount dependency, not just "the network is slow" — is what separates a real diagnosis from a guess.
